object.medium: Nocturne for solo piano; engraved first edition
object.description: Chopin wrote the three Nocturnes of Opus 9 between 1830 and 1832, in the years he left Warsaw for Vienna and then settled in Paris, and they were his first nocturnes to be published, in Leipzig and Paris in 1832-33. He dedicated them to Marie Pleyel, the pianist wife of his publisher and piano maker Camille Pleyel. The second, in E-flat major, is the most played piece he ever wrote: a slow waltz-like accompaniment under a singing melody that returns three times, each time more elaborately ornamented, in the manner of an Italian opera aria. It fixed the idea of the nocturne, a short night piece for piano, that John Field had invented. The sheet shown is the title page of the Paris first edition issued by Maurice Schlesinger. The visitor hears the nocturne played by Frank Lévy in a Musopen recording released into the public domain.
facts: The nocturnes were printed by Kistner in Leipzig and Schlesinger in Paris in 1832-33, and by Wessel in London.
Chopin's pupils recorded many of his own improvised variants of the ornaments, so no two early editions agree on every note.
The dedicatee, Marie Pleyel (née Moke), was a celebrated virtuoso who had earlier been engaged to Berlioz.
